lesson_title: Gaps That Grow: Quadratic Number Patterns
hook_text: The can stacks go 1, 3, 6, 10 — can any stack hold exactly 100 cans? The difference table already knows the answer.
clip_script: Cans stacked in triangles: 1, then 3, then 6, then 10. Measure the gaps: 2, 3, 4 — not equal, but growing by exactly 1 each time. That constant gap-of-gaps is the second difference, and it means the pattern is quadratic: T n equals a n squared plus b n plus c. Three sentences build the formula. Half the second difference is a. The first gap equals 3 a plus b. The first term equals a plus b plus c. Here that gives half n squared plus half n — stack n holds n times n plus one, over two. Now the exam question: can a stack hold exactly 100 cans? Stack thirteen holds 91. Stack fourteen holds 105. The stacks jump from 91 straight over 100 to 105 — and the algebra agrees, because solving for n gives no natural number. When n refuses to come out whole, the value is simply not in the pattern, and saying that in a sentence is the mark. Gaps, then gaps of gaps, three sentences for the formula, and n must be whole.
visual_style: Shop-front can pyramids growing stack by stack, a difference table drawn under them with the second row lighting up, a 100-can order slip sliding between stacks 13 and 14 and falling through the gap.
pacing: Quick counts through the stacks, a beat on the growing gaps, a hard stop on the 100-can order, calm certainty on the close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and build the general term of any quadratic pattern in three sentences.
